rationale: The fold check shows that the modeled GRIN2D–GPR6 interface spans both cytoplasmic and extracellular residues. That is topologically impossible across an intact membrane, so the large interface (3225 Å², 639 contacts, interface pLDDT 63.7) is most likely an artifact of folding two transmembrane proteins as free sequences. This undercuts my earlier LIKELY_SUBCOMPLEX call. That call treated the missing GRIN1 subunit as the main caveat and ignored the topology problem. Adding GRIN1 would not fix a contact that is impossible in the membrane. The rest of the evidence is unchanged and gives no independent support: STRING and CellPhoneDB have no entry for the pair, PubMed co-occurrence is 0, and the supplied ipTM of 0.67 is only moderate. Brain co-expression of the two proteins is the only argument left, and it does not outweigh a fold that violates membrane topology. Glycosylation is a minor point here, because the interface itself is topologically invalid.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: GRIN2D is a glycoprotein with 6 glycosylation sites. GPR6 is a glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites and is palmitoylated. This is secondary to the topology violation, and no per-residue interface data were available.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 hits for GRIN2D together with GPR6.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING: no association. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction, and GPR6 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. The known_interaction_strength check is "none", so the pair is novel but has no literature support.
follow_up: Only if there is a specific biological reason to suspect a GRIN2D–GPR6 interaction: re-fold with GRIN1 and a second GluN2 subunit, then check that any interface lies within a single topological compartment (for example transmembrane-helix contacts only).

rationale: The pair is novel in every database checked (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, 0 PubMed co-mentions) and the fold is partner-specific (confident against 1 of 9 receptors tested, ipTM 0.64, interface PAE 2.13 A). However, EFNA3 (P52797) is a GPI-anchored glycoprotein (1 lipidation site, 3 glycosylation sites) and GPR21 (Q99679) is a glycosylated 7-TM orphan GPCR (2 glycosylation sites). The 587-token complex equals the two full-length precursors (238 + 349 residues), so the fold appears to include EFNA3's signal peptide and GPI propeptide, which are cleaved from the mature protein. A buried surface of 5310 A^2 with 1124 contacts is far more than a GPCR's small extracellular face can offer a roughly 200-residue ephrin ectodomain. My inference, not confirmed by a fold, is that hydrophobic precursor segments or glycan-bearing regions are packed against the transmembrane bundle, an interface that would not exist in vivo.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: UniProt lists EFNA3 with the keywords Glycoprotein, GPI-anchor and Lipoprotein, and with 3 glycosylation sites, 1 lipidation site (the GPI attachment, which replaces the cleaved C-terminal propeptide) and 2 disulfide bonds. GPR21 carries the keyword Glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites, which for a GPCR are expected on the extracellular N-terminus or loops, the only surface an ephrin could reach. The PubMed PTM searches (11 hits for EFNA3, 1 for GPR21) returned nothing specifically about glycosylation; the titles concern miR-210-3p/EFNA3 signalling and plasmalogen signalling through orphan GPCRs. Whether the glycosylation sites or the cleaved signal and GPI propeptides sit on the modeled interface is unverified. The very large interface (5310 A^2) and its moderate interface pLDDT of 68.4 make this plausible.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence for EFNA3 and GPR21 returned 0 hits.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING returned no association for the pair. CellPhoneDB returned no curated interaction, and GPR21 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table. PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 papers. The pair is unreported. UniProt describes EFNA3's function as a ligand for Eph receptor tyrosine kinases, and GPR21 as an orphan receptor.
follow_up:
fold_complex was not available in this run. Recommended next steps:
1. Re-fold using mature EFNA3 only (signal peptide and C-terminal GPI propeptide removed) against GPR21, and check whether ipTM stays at or above 0.5.
2. Inspect the interface topology on GPR21. The contacts must be Extracellular, with or without the transmembrane boundary; any Cytoplasmic or lipid-facing transmembrane contacts would mark an artifact.
3. Check whether the 3 EFNA3 and 2 GPR21 N-glycosylation sites fall on the interface. If they do, re-fold with the glycans attached.
4. Check whether the modeled surface on EFNA3 overlaps its Eph-receptor-binding loop, for example by folding with EPHA2 as a competitor. EPHA2 is suggested as a canonical ephrin-A receptor from general knowledge, not from a tool result.
5. If the interface survives these checks, test binding at the bench with EFNA3-Fc on GPR21-expressing cells.

rationale: The fold check shows the IGF2–GPRC5C interface sits on the cytoplasmic face of GPRC5C. IGF2 is a secreted hormone with no cytosolic surface, so it cannot physically meet that face. This undercuts my earlier compartment-plausibility argument, which assumed IGF2 would contact the extracellular side. The same fold also places a glycosylation or lipidation site directly on the modeled interface. AF3 does not represent glycans, so the bare-sequence contact is unreliable even if the interface were extracellular. I had left this as an unresolved caveat, but it now falls on the interface itself. The weak breadth-control signal (1 of 17 receptors, ipTM 0.49, interface pLDDT 64.7) does not offset a wrong-topology pose. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed all show no prior evidence, so the pair is not known. Tissue co-expression plausibility alone does not rescue a pose on the wrong side of the membrane.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: GPRC5C is a glycoprotein with 1 annotated glycosylation site. The fold places that site on the modeled interface, so a glycan-dependent or lipidation-dependent contact is likely not represented by AF3. The IGF2 UniProt lookup returned the wrong entry, so no PTM data was obtained for the real ligand.
cooccurrence_evidence: pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 hits for IGF2 and GPRC5C together.
known_interaction_evidence: No STRING association, no CellPhoneDB entry (GPRC5C is absent from its gene table) and 0 PubMed co-occurrence papers. The pair is not already known.
follow_up: Optionally re-fold IGF2 against the GPRC5C extracellular domain only, and check whether a pose on the extracellular face holds up, ideally with glycan-aware modeling.

rationale: The AF3 fold put GNRH2 in contact with both cytoplasmic and extracellular residues of MRGPRX2. A secreted ligand cannot touch both faces of an intact membrane receptor, so the modeled interface is physically invalid and cannot support CONFIRMED_NOVEL. The likely cause is that AF3 was given the 85-aa prohormone, whose GAP region and signal peptide are not part of the bioactive ligand. The real ligand is the processed, amidated decapeptide. Other evidence is unchanged: STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence are all negative, and HPA rates the pair plausible (secreted hormone versus mast-cell membrane GPCR). MRGPRX2 is also a promiscuous receptor for cationic, amphipathic peptides, and the GnRH-II decapeptide fits that profile, so the hypothesis is still reasonable. It rests on pharmacophore reasoning only and has no valid structural support, so I am downgrading to INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than IMPLAUSIBLE.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: Neither protein has glycosylation sites. GNRH2 is C-terminally amidated and proteolytically processed, with an N-terminal pyroglutamate in the mature peptide. A bare prohormone fold does not represent this and may explain the spurious cytoplasmic/extracellular contacts.
cooccurrence_evidence: pubmed_cooccurrence count = 0; no papers mention both genes.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING found=false, CellPhoneDB found=false, PubMed co-occurrence 0 hits. There is no prior literature on this pair, so it remains novel in the literature sense (known_interaction_strength=none).
follow_up: Re-fold MRGPRX2 with only the mature GnRH-II decapeptide (pGlu-HWSHGWYPG-NH2), representing the pyroGlu and C-terminal amidation where possible. Then check that the interface is restricted to the extracellular vestibule and TM-bundle orthosteric pocket. Compare against known MRGPRX2 peptide agonist poses (for example substance P or cortistatin-14).

rationale: GHRL's UniProt entry (Q9UBU3) states that octanoylated ghrelin-28 is the predominant form and that "octanoylation is essential for the activation of the growth hormone secretagogue receptor type 1 (GHSR)" — the protein carries 3 Lipidation features and the keyword "Lipoprotein", a lipid-mediated binding mechanism AF3's bare-sequence fold cannot represent at all, so the modeled ipTM=0.65 interface is of an unacylated peptide that in vivo would present a very different pharmacophore. MRGPRX4 (Q96LA9) is moreover documented as a receptor for a chemically unrelated ligand class — bile acids, with a preference for 3-sulfated bile acids such as deoxycholate 3-sulfate — not for peptide hormones, and it carries 2 N-glycosylation sites on its extracellular face where a peptide would have to dock. No prior literature or database links the pair.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: GHRL UniProt ptm_topology_feature_counts: Lipidation 3, Modified residue 1; keywords include "Lipoprotein" and "Amidation"; FUNCTION explicitly makes Ser3 octanoylation essential for receptor activation. MRGPRX4 UniProt: Glycosylation 2, Disulfide bond 2, keyword "Glycoprotein" — the glycans sit on the extracellular/loop face that any peptide ligand would contact. PubMed PTM search for GHRL returned 5 mostly irrelevant hits (tau neuropathology, chicken bursal B-cells); for MRGPRX4, 2 hits including PMID 38718132 on phospho-drug-associated pruritus, i.e. its ligand recognition is sensitive to ligand chemical modification state. AF3 modeled neither the octanoyl chain nor the receptor glycans.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING: no association found for GHRL-MRGPRX4 (found=false, no channels). CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction (found=false); MRGPRX4 is not even in the CellPhoneDB gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. So the pair is genuinely unreported — novelty is not the issue here, mechanism is.
follow_up: Re-run AF3 (or AlphaFold3 with CCD-defined modified residue) with ghrelin's Ser3 n-octanoyl group represented and with N-glycans at MRGPRX4's two annotated sites, and check whether the interface survives and whether a glycosylation site lands on the modeled contact surface — I could not run fold_complex/resolve_ptm_artifact in this run. Also check the pose location: a genuine MRGPRX4 agonist contacts the transmembrane bundle (bile-acid orthosteric pocket), so a ghrelin peptide resting only on extracellular loops would be a negative result. Wet-lab test: Ca2+/IP1 assay of acyl- and des-acyl-ghrelin on MRGPRX4-expressing cells versus the bile-acid positive control deoxycholate 3-sulfate.

rationale: The fold check shows two problems that my earlier LIKELY_SUBCOMPLEX verdict ignored. (1) Topology violation: the AF3 interface is on GPR101's cytoplasmic face, but FGA is a secreted plasma protein with no cytosolic localisation and no membrane topology. A secreted fibrinogen chain cannot physically reach the intracellular side of a plasma-membrane GPCR, so the predicted contact is geometrically impossible in vivo. (2) A glycosylation/lipidation site lies directly on the modeled interface. AF3 does not represent these modifications, so the contact is likely a bare-sequence artifact. This is secondary to the topology problem, and I had previously treated it as an unresolved caveat. The earlier missing-subunit argument (FGA is normally part of the FGA/FGB/FGG hexamer) still applies, but it is now a minor point. Supporting evidence is also weak: STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed all show no record of the pair (known_interaction_strength=none), and ipTM is 0.53 with interface pLDDT 68.8. HPA compartment plausibility ('plausible') only means the proteins could meet extracellularly. It does not rescue an interface modeled on the cytoplasmic face. I am therefore downgrading to IMPLAUSIBLE at medium confidence, since the topology flag comes from a single automated fold analysis.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: FGA is glycosylated and phosphorylated, and GPR101 is glycosylated. The fold flags a glycosylation/lipidation site directly on the modeled interface, which AF3 cannot represent. This further undermines the predicted contact.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence for FGA and GPR101 returned 0 hits.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence (0 hits) all show no record of FGA-GPR101. GPR101 is an orphan receptor. known_interaction_strength=none.
follow_up: If this pair is of interest, re-model the extracellular domain of GPR101 with the full fibrinogen hexamer (FGA, FGB, FGG) and with glycans. Check whether the interface moves to an extracellular face.

rationale: The fold check shows the modeled FGFR1–GPR50 interface covers both cytoplasmic and extracellular residues. That is topologically impossible across an intact membrane, so the large 7088 Å² interface (ipTM 0.38, interface pLDDT 64.7) is probably an artifact of folding two membrane proteins without a bilayer. Low interface PAE does not fix this. The check also found a glycosylation or lipidation site directly on the interface, and FGFR1's extracellular glycans are not represented in AF3, so any extracellular contact is unreliable too. The pair has no literature, STRING or CellPhoneDB support, and HPA plausibility is unknown. The only positive points are that both are plasma-membrane receptors and that GPR50 binds TGFBR1, which is an analogy and not evidence for FGFR1. I am moving from INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE to IMPLAUSIBLE because the only structural evidence is internally inconsistent and nothing independent supports the pair. Confidence is medium because a real interaction, such as a transmembrane or cytoplasmic one, is not excluded. It is simply not shown by this fold.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: FGFR1 has 8 extracellular glycosylation sites. The fold check places a glycosylation or lipidation site directly on the modeled interface, and AF3 does not represent glycans, so the modeled contact cannot be trusted.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence for FGFR1 and GPR50 returned 0 hits.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence (0 papers) all report nothing for this pair (known_interaction_strength=none). GPR50's binding to TGFBR1 is only an analogy.
follow_up: Re-fold only the plausible same-side segments, such as the FGFR1 and GPR50 cytoplasmic or transmembrane regions, or fold with a membrane-aware method. Test experimentally with co-IP or proximity ligation in pituitary or lactotroph cells.

rationale: WNT3 (secreted) and the orphan GPCR GPR101 (cell membrane per UniProt) are a compartment-plausible ligand-receptor pair with no prior record in STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed (0 co-mentions), so the pair is novel. However, WNT3 is a lipoprotein and glycoprotein (UniProt P56703: 1 lipidation site, 2 glycosylation sites), and GPR101 (Q96P66) carries 2 glycosylation sites; Wnt receptor engagement is known to depend on the lipid adduct, which AF3's bare-sequence model does not represent. Combined with a marginal ipTM of 0.55, interface pLDDT of 67.7 and p_twoway of 0.0528, the modelled interface cannot be trusted as drawn. No fold was available in this run to check whether the modification sites sit on the interface.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: WNT3 (UniProt P56703): keywords Glycoprotein and Lipoprotein; feature counts are 1 lipidation, 2 glycosylation and 11 disulfide bonds. The PubMed PTM search returned 52 hits, including PMID 38994173, "N-glycosylation of Wnt3 regulates the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma by affecting Wnt/β-catenin signal pathway". GPR101 (UniProt Q96P66): keyword Glycoprotein; 2 glycosylation sites and 1 disulfide bond; the PubMed PTM search returned 1 hit, which is not about GPR101 glycosylation. The WNT3 lipid adduct and the glycans on both proteins are extracellular and plausibly relevant to an extracellular ligand-receptor interface, and none of them is represented in the AF3 model. Whether any of these sites lies on the modelled interface is unverified.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence for WNT3 and GPR101 returned 0 hits.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING returned no association for WNT3 and GPR101. CellPhoneDB returned no curated interaction, and GPR101 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table. PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 papers. There is no prior report of this pair. UniProt describes WNT3 as a ligand for frizzled-family seven-transmembrane receptors and GPR101 as an orphan receptor.
other_subunits: FZD family receptor (one representative, e.g. FZD8);LRP6
follow_up: 1) Run an AF3 fold of WNT3 with GPR101 and inspect the structural analysis: confirm the interface falls on GPR101 extracellular or transmembrane-boundary residues (not cytoplasmic), and check whether the WNT3 lipidation site, the 2 WNT3 N-glycosylation sites or the 2 GPR101 glycosylation sites lie on the interface. 2) If a glycosylation site is on the interface, re-fold with the core glycan attached; also re-fold with the WNT3 lipid modification represented. 3) As a specificity control, compare against WNT3 folded with one frizzled receptor (its known receptor class), with and without the co-receptor LRP6. The supplied breadth data (1 of 5 receptors tested was confident) argues against a fully non-specific WNT3 surface, but p_twoway of 0.0528 is borderline. 4) Wet-lab: a binding assay using properly lipidated, secreted WNT3 on GPR101-expressing cells, and a GPR101 Gs/cAMP readout.

rationale: The real AF3 fold flagged a topology violation: the modelled A-B interface spans both cytoplasmic and extracellular residues, which cannot happen across an intact membrane. That undermines the structural support. Together with the earlier ipTM of 0.47 and the near-clash distance of 1.77 A, the pose is probably a bare-sequence artifact and not a real contact, so I withdraw CONFIRMED_NOVEL. The biological case is unchanged: both proteins are brain and oligodendrocyte membrane proteins linked to myelination, and STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed return nothing for the pair. Because the case rests on co-expression and shared function and not on the pose, this is a possible indirect association within a myelin-associated surface complex (CADM4 with CADM2/3 and MAG) and not a validated direct interaction. The 3 glycosylation sites on each protein add further uncertainty, since AF3 does not model glycans.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: CADM4 and GPR37 each have 3 annotated glycosylation sites, mostly extracellular. CADM4 is also palmitoylated. AF3 models none of these, so any extracellular ectodomain contact could differ from the bare-protein pose.
cooccurrence_evidence: pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 papers mentioning CADM4 and GPR37 together.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence (0 papers) all returned nothing for this pair, so it is not known. Known-interaction strength is none.
follow_up: Re-run the fold with CADM2, CADM3 and MAG as extra subunits, restricted to the extracellular domains. Check that any interface is topologically valid, meaning extracellular-only or transmembrane-compatible. Consider an experimental co-IP in oligodendrocytes.

rationale: I'm downgrading from CONFIRMED_NOVEL for two reasons. (1) Both proteins sit in the plasma membrane, but HPA shows no shared tissue-level protein expression, and neither is secreted. The bone-marrow MSC RNA overlap I relied on is RNA-only, so it doesn't show the proteins meet in the same cell. Without protein-level co-expression, I have no substantiated route for contact. (2) The real AF3 fold's 6079 Å^2 interface spans both cytoplasmic and extracellular residues. That is topologically impossible across an intact membrane, so the confident-looking pose (ipTM 0.66, interface pLDDT 60) is a bare-sequence artifact, not a real contact. The pair still has no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed trace, so it isn't a known interaction. But the lack of prior evidence plus no co-expression plus a topology-violating fold leaves no support for a real interaction.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: ROR2 has 3 glycosylation sites and MRGPRF has 1. Neither is a lectin. Glycosylation is a minor caveat here, and the topology violation is the main problem.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence for ROR2 and MRGPRF returned 0 hits.
known_interaction_evidence: No STRING association, no CellPhoneDB curated interaction (MRGPRF isn't in the gene table), and 0 PubMed co-occurrence papers. The pair is not known, but absence of prior evidence gives no positive support either.
follow_up: Folding tools were not available in this run. Recommended next steps: (1) Re-fold ROR2 + MRGPRF and read the interface topology for both chains, to confirm the 6079 A^2 interface does not combine Cytoplasmic and Extracellular residues at once (AF3 models no lipid bilayer, so a large interface between a single-pass RTK and a 7TM GPCR is at risk of this), and to check whether any of the 3 ROR2 or 1 MRGPRF N-glycosylation sites sit on the interface; if one does, re-fold with the glycan attached. (2) Counter-screen for specificity: only 1 partner receptor was tested (1 of 1 confident), so fold ROR2 against two or three unrelated class A GPCRs, including other MRGPR family members, and fold MRGPRF against ROR1 and an unrelated single-pass RTK. (3) Optionally fold with WNT5A, the ROR2 ligand named in UniProt (CellPhoneDB lists no curated complex for ROR2, so this is a suggestion and not a known missing subunit). (4) Wet-lab: co-immunoprecipitation or proximity ligation in bone marrow MSCs or smooth muscle cells, where both are expressed.

rationale: Compartment and novelty checks support the pair: LGALS3 is secreted and at the plasma membrane, GPR39 is a cell-surface GPCR, and STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed show no known interaction. However, UniProt describes Galectin-3 (P17931) as a "Galactose-specific lectin" and GPR39 (O43194) as a Glycoprotein with 3 annotated glycosylation sites, so any real galectin-3 binding to GPR39 would most likely be glycan-mediated, which AF3's bare-sequence model cannot represent. The fold itself is only borderline (ipTM 0.53, interface pLDDT 66.8), so the modeled protein-protein interface is not reliable evidence of a real contact surface.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: UniProt describes LGALS3 (P17931) as a "Galactose-specific lectin" with the keyword Lectin, meaning its documented binding mechanism to cell-surface partners is through beta-galactoside glycans. UniProt lists GPR39 (O43194) with the keyword Glycoprotein and 3 annotated Glycosylation features; for a GPCR these are expected on the extracellular N-terminus or loops, although the per-residue positions were not checked. This is directly relevant to the interface: the real contact would be lectin-to-glycan, and the glycans could also sterically occupy the modeled protein surface. The PubMed PTM searches (39 hits for LGALS3, 25 for GPR39) returned mostly non-specific titles and added nothing site-specific.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed returned 1 co-mention (PMID 40616194, Clin Epigenetics 2025, DNA methylation and transcriptional profiling in bronchopulmonary dysplasia). This looks unrelated to a direct interaction between the two proteins.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING returned no association for LGALS3 and GPR39. CellPhoneDB returned no curated interaction. PubMed co-occurrence returned 1 hit (PMID 40616194, a methylation and transcriptional profiling study of hyperoxia-induced bronchopulmonary dysplasia), which is a co-mention in an omics gene list and not a report of binding. The pair is therefore unreported as a direct interaction.
follow_up: No fold could be run in this triage, so three checks remain. (1) Re-fold LGALS3 with GPR39 and confirm whether the interface sits on GPR39's extracellular residues and whether any of the 3 UniProt N-glycosylation sites lie on it; if so, re-fold with the core glycan attached. (2) Inspect the supplied model for clashes, since the minimum separation of 2.21 A with 863 contacts and a buried surface of 3905 A^2 is suspiciously tight for an ipTM of only 0.53 and an interface pLDDT of 66.8. (3) Test at the bench whether galectin-3 binding to GPR39-expressing cells is abolished by lactose or a galectin-3 CRD inhibitor, or by PNGase F treatment or glycosylation-site mutants of GPR39; this would separate glycan-dependent binding from a true protein-protein contact. The supplied breadth screen (1 of 5 partner receptors confident, p_twoway = 0.033) suggests some specificity to GPR39, which makes the glycan-dependent hypothesis worth testing and not simply discarding. HTR1A and GALR1 are listed as other subunits only because UniProt reports GPR39 forms heteroreceptor complexes with them; CellPhoneDB lists no complex for either protein and there is no evidence they are required for this pair.

rationale: I'm changing the verdict from LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM to IMPLAUSIBLE, because the contradiction is valid and the PTM explanation was the weaker of the two concerns. Neither GFRA3 nor GPR37L1 is secreted, and HPA shows zero shared protein-level tissue or cell-type expression, so the data give no route for the two to meet. The fold check also flagged a topology violation, and the AF3 support is already borderline (ipTM 0.51, interface pLDDT 65.4, 2.0 Å minimum separation). The 3488 Å^2 interface is probably a bare-sequence modeling artifact. Glycosylation on both proteins (3 sites on GFRA3, 6 on GPR37L1) could be a secondary confound, but it isn't needed to explain the result. There is also no prior evidence for the pair: STRING and CellPhoneDB returned nothing and PubMed co-occurrence found 0 papers. That absence supports novelty only in the sense that nobody has reported it. It doesn't offset the lack of any co-localization.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: GFRA3 has 3 glycosylation sites plus a GPI anchor. GPR37L1 has 6 glycosylation sites, and its N-terminus is MMP-processed (PMID 33203955). Glycans are a possible confound for the interface, but whether any site sits on it was not established. This is secondary to the topology and co-localization problems.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence for GFRA3 and GPR37L1 returned 0 hits.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING: no association. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. The pair is unreported, but with no co-expression this doesn't make it plausible.
follow_up: If this pair is still of interest, test it with RET included and with membrane topology constraints. First look for a cell type or tissue where both proteins are actually expressed.

rationale: PTN (secreted growth factor) and GPR22 (orphan Gi/Go GPCR) are a compartment-plausible ligand/receptor pair, both brain-expressed, with no prior report in STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed (0 co-mentions), so the pair is novel. However, UniProt describes PTN's receptor binding as mediated by chondroitin sulfate glycan chains on proteoglycan receptors, and GPR22 carries 2 annotated glycosylation sites and the Glycoprotein keyword; AF3 models neither. The structural support is also marginal: ipTM 0.45 is below the 0.5 convention despite interface PAE 2.67 A and interface pLDDT 70.9, and the minimum separation of 1.82 A suggests an un-relaxed, near-clashing interface.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: UniProt PTN (P21246): the function text states it "binds cell-surface proteoglycan receptor via their chondroitin sulfate (CS) groups" and it carries the Heparin-binding keyword. Its documented receptor-binding mechanism is therefore largely glycosaminoglycan-mediated, which a bare-sequence AF3 fold cannot represent, although UniProt also notes non-proteoglycan receptors such as ALK. PTN itself has no annotated glycosylation (5 disulfide bonds only). UniProt GPR22 (Q99680): Glycoprotein keyword and 2 annotated glycosylation sites, which were not modeled; whether they lie on the modeled interface (buried surface area 2427 A2) is unknown. The pubmed_ptm_glycosylation searches were uninformative: 84 hits for PTN and 2 for GPR22, with none of the returned titles addressing glycosylation of either protein.
cooccurrence_evidence: pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 hits for PTN together with GPR22.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction (GPR22 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. No hit in any of the three sources, so the pair is not previously reported. GPR22 is an orphan receptor per UniProt.
follow_up: A fold could not be run in this triage. Recommended: (1) re-fold PTN + GPR22 with AF3 and read the interface topology, to confirm the contact is on GPR22's extracellular N-terminus/loops and not its cytoplasmic side, and to check whether either of the 2 GPR22 glycosylation sites sits on the interface; if one does, re-fold with the core N-glycan attached. (2) Counter-screen PTN against unrelated GPCRs, because PTN is a highly basic heparin-binding protein prone to non-specific electrostatic contacts; the supplied breadth data (1 of 4 receptors confident, p_twoway = 0.033) argue for some specificity but come from only 4 receptors. (3) Inspect the 1.82 A minimum separation for clashes. (4) If the pose survives, test in the wet lab with PTN stimulation of GPR22-expressing cells using a Gi/Go cAMP-inhibition readout, with and without chondroitinase/heparinase treatment to separate protein-mediated from glycosaminoglycan-mediated binding. PTPRZ1 and SDC3 are listed as known PTN proteoglycan co-receptors from UniProt, not as CellPhoneDB complex members (no CellPhoneDB complex was found for either protein).

rationale: NMS is a secreted brain neuropeptide and GPR158 is a brain-enriched plasma-membrane GPCR, so a paracrine ligand-receptor pairing is compartmentally plausible, and STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed (0 papers) all show no prior record of this pair. Support from the fold itself is only marginal: ipTM is 0.56 and interface pLDDT is 56.0, although interface PAE is 2.69 A and only 1 of the 3 receptors NMS was tested against passed the confidence gate. No fold could be run here, so it is unchecked whether the interface is on the extracellular side or whether any of GPR158's 5 glycosylation sites sits on it; the very large interface (5202 A^2, 1117 contacts) also suggests the full NMS precursor was folded and not the mature amidated peptide.
ptm_glycosylation_evidence: UniProt annotates GPR158 as a Glycoprotein with 5 glycosylation sites, 2 disulfide bonds and 6 modified residues (Phosphoprotein, Ubl conjugation). Glycosylation sites on a GPCR are expected to be extracellular, which is where a secreted peptide would bind, so a glycan at the modeled interface is possible but could not be checked without a fold. NMS carries the keywords Amidation and Cleavage on pair of basic residues, with 1 modified residue: the active form is a processed, C-terminally amidated peptide that AF3 did not represent. The PubMed PTM search for NMS (61 hits) was dominated by unrelated uses of the abbreviation (e.g. native mass spectrometry) and is uninformative; the 3 hits for GPR158 concern its neuronal function, not its glycosylation.
cooccurrence_evidence: PubMed co-occurrence for NMS and GPR158 returned 0 hits.
known_interaction_evidence: STRING returned no association for NMS-GPR158. CellPhoneDB returned no curated interaction, and GPR158 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table.
